question: A normal chest X-ray obtained within the first hour of kerosene ingestion reliably excludes aspiration pneumonitis and can be used to justify early discharge.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Radiological infiltrates in aspiration pneumonitis typically take 4–6 hours to appear after kerosene ingestion. A child with normal early CXR but persistent cough, tachypnoea, or reduced saturations must be observed and have a repeat CXR at 4–6 hours before any decision about discharge.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Incorrect — this statement is false. A chest X-ray obtained within the first 1–4 hours of kerosene ingestion may be normal even when clinically significant aspiration has occurred, because radiological changes lag behind clinical toxicity by 4–6 hours. A normal early CXR does NOT exclude aspiration and should never be the sole basis for discharge.
